title: Dynamical spectral functions from bitstring-sampled quantum subspaces: entanglement, not one-body magic, tracks the sampling cost
abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) and quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) are the electronic-structure methods with most hardware traction, yet their canonical target -- the ground-state energy -- is where classical methods have caught up. We move the target to dynamics and the resource question. From one bitstring-sampling primitive -- computational-basis measurements of a shallow real-time circuit, with no Hadamard or controlled unitaries -- we reconstruct, from sampled subspaces, the single-particle spectral functions $A(ω)$ and $A(k,ω)$ and the neutral-sector dynamical structure factors $S(q,ω)$ and $S^{zz}(q,ω)$, each built classically in the Lehmann representation from its own subspace. The reconstruction matches exact diagonalization on Hubbard chains and, for $A(ω)$, across nineteen molecules (FCI-verified to $<10^{-5}$ Ha), and runs on the IBM Heron processor. Second, we ask which resource controls the cost -- the determinant support $|\mathcal{S}|$ the sampler must populate. On number-conserving states the fermionic AntiFlatness collapses to one 1-RDM invariant, $\mathcal{F}_1 = 4\,\mathrm{tr}[γ(1-γ)] = 2N_u$. An orbital-rotation (Gaussian) invariant while $|\mathcal{S}|$ is basis dependent, $\mathcal{F}_1$ is provably decoupled from the cost; the cost is instead lower-bounded and tracked by the entanglement -- the minimal bond dimension $χ$ (Spearman $ρ= 0.90$). One-body magic is thus a faithful multireference diagnostic but an unreliable cost predictor; any genuine advantage lives in the non-Gaussianity of the higher-body cumulants. We prove moment exactness and a sampling bound polynomial in $|\mathcal{S}|$, independent of Hilbert-space dimension. Self-consistent configuration recovery improves the subspace under device noise, while a learned generative model does not beat that classical baseline.
summary: This work develops a method to calculate dynamic properties, such as spectral functions, in strongly correlated electron systems using limited quantum resources. By sampling subspaces via simple measurements, the authors show that the computational cost is dictated by entanglement structure ($\chi$), not by easily measurable one-body quantities. This advances the field by providing a resource-aware roadmap for simulating complex electronic dynamics on current hardware.
main_problem: To extend quantum subspace diagonalization from static ground-state energies to continuous, frequency-resolved dynamics for electronic structure calculations.
main_result: The sampling cost is governed by the entanglement (minimal bond dimension $\chi$), not by one-body invariants like Fermionic AntiFlatness ($F_1$).
method: Reconstruct spectral functions and dynamical structure factors classically from sampled subspaces using only computational-basis measurements on a quantum processor.
model_or_system: The methods are applied to electronic structure problems, validated against Hubbard chains and molecular systems, focusing on charged and neutral sectors of many-electron Hamiltonians.
key_observables: Single-particle spectral functions $A(\omega)$, momentum-resolved $A(k, \omega)$, and dynamical structure factors $S(q, \omega)$.
important_parameters: The resource cost is tracked by the determinant support size $|\mathcal{S}|$ and lower-bounded by entanglement ($\chi$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes moment exactness can be achieved with a sampling bound polynomial in $|\mathcal{S}|$, independent of Hilbert-space dimension.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the methodology by moving the target from ground state to dynamics, details the reconstruction process using shallow measurements, and then analyzes the resource cost, contrasting one-body diagnostics with entanglement measures.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete pathway for simulating complex many-body dynamics (like spectral functions) on near-term quantum hardware by identifying the true scaling bottleneck (entanglement) rather than relying on simplified local observables.
